## Introduction

I have been thinking about minimalism in language modeling and how one might transfer lessons learned from coding models to chain of thought (COT) reasoning agents.

## TL;DR - Constraints Boost Creativity

1. Contained resources and a compact lexicon can make language modeling much easier. []{.column-margin}
1. A Simple Formal grammars particularly simple ones can make a small language model perform well
1. boundaries make the world a lot easier to model.

>     There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.  -- Phil Karlton

1. *Variable names* and *function names* and **comments** are the high cardinality elements of code.
However these are also the parts that make it possible to effectively ground the code in natural language and human concepts. However if we can reduce thier cardinality and ambiguity using a controlled vocabulary and a simple grammar, we might actually boost the overall ability of a agent to understand and generate code.
1. The same ideas might apply to a reasoning agent. 
1. A COT could benefit greatly from being grounded in a compact controlled vocabulary.
1. It would could also use simple grammars. 
1. Better yet if the chain of thought could be was structured so it could be interpreted as code or rendered as prose.
1. Better yet if the COT followed some established patterns like:
    - inductive/deductive reasoning
    - syllogisms
    - propositional logic
    - predicate logic
    - first-order logic
    - modal logic
    - probabilistic reasoning
    - Decision trees 
    - [McKinsey's MECE framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MECE_principle)
    - Frames and scripts from cognitive science
    - Planning
    - etc.

## Advantages of Coding Agents

- One advantage of coding agents is that they operate in a much more constrained environment than general language models.
- The grammar of a programming language is often much simpler than that of a natural language — it is usually easier to parse or interpret.
- APIs provide clearly defined boundaries.
- Coding agents often perform well in constrained scenarios but can fail in production when capabilities must handle high cardinality. [Michael Stonebraker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Stonebraker) pointed out that LLMs struggle with text-to-SQL in data warehouses because such schemas can have many tables and columns with similar or duplicated names.

## Two Languages: Natural vs Programming

Suppose we have two languages:

- A natural language with a million words and a complex grammar.
- A typed programming language with ~100 words and a simple grammar (think Lisp). If we shorten identifiers in the code (e.g., variable and function names) to a compact, regular form we can keep even long programs within a small lexicon. (Recall that LLMs tokenize input into fixed tokens and represent them as numbers; this is about streamlining that process.)

## Normalizing Code: Trade-offs

There are two main downsides to normalizing code:

1. We lose grounding in natural language.
2. We introduce ambiguity from many equivalent programs that differ only by identifier names.

The core issue is that many programs can be equivalent while using different variable and function names; a model must learn that these variants represent the same program, or it may incorrectly associate common names with particular behaviors.

## Training Implications

Building an LLM with similar perplexity for both languages will require far fewer parameters for the second (programming) language. Consequently, it will need fewer tokens and less computation to train.

In practice we also want the programming model to understand queries and comments in natural language. As soon as we add natural language, however, we lose some of the benefits described above.

## Combining Models: A Possible Approach

Can we combine the two models to get the best of both worlds? One idea is to use embeddings in the code to bridge representations between the compact, formal program space and natural language.

## Conclusion

This note sketches trade-offs between compact program representations and natural language grounding; next steps include concrete experiments with normalization, embedding strategies, and hybrid model architectures.

## Experiments to Try

1. Create an additional skill that enforces the 53 writing rules of the ASD-STE100 standard.
1. create a prompt to translate text to ASD-STE100 compliant text.
1. Create a small extensions to support linked data entities in the ASD-STE100 compliant text.
1. Convert a corpus of technical texts & code to ASD-STE100 compliant text.
1. Train a reasoning language model on the two version.
